title: What the Fed Hears and What It Concludes: Supply-Chain Narratives and U.S. Inflation Forecasting ⋆
abstract: This paper constructs audited, sentence-level measures of supply-chain narratives in two complementary Federal Reserve information sets: the Beige Book, which records what regional contacts report, and minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which record national-level policy deliberation. The corpus contains 230,555 sentences from 472 documents spanning 1997-2025. A high-recall transformer screens for supply-chain relevance, and a separately frozen narrative model produces source-specific monthly narrative shares. Both stages are evaluated using protected, probability-stratified audits with design weights. I then test whether these measures add predictive information in a historical holdout exercise using hybrid inflationforecasting systems that combine a Minnesota-prior Bayesian vector autoregression with an XGBoost residual correction. Relative to an otherwise identical no-text hybrid, adding FOMC narratives lowers core-inflation RMSE by approximately 2.3 percent at one month, 6.4 percent at six months, and 6.5 percent at twelve months. The pattern is strongly source-specific: FOMC narratives lower RMSE at every horizon examined, whereas Beige Book narratives provide little or no systematic improvement. The evidence therefore points to source-specific predictive content in Federal Reserve supply-chain narratives rather than a generic forecasting benefit from adding textual information.
why: Fed narratives for inflation; NLP on real financial text, rigorous audited methodology

title: Order Invariance at the Last Language-Model Boundary: A Pre-Registered Test of an LLM Evidence Synthesizer Inside a Deterministic Trading Architecture
abstract: Large language models are known to be sensitive to the order in which they read their inputs. How much that sensitivity matters once a model sits inside a trading system whose final decision is made by deterministic code is not known. This paper reports a pre-registered test at the only point in a production multi-agent trading architecture (ZVAKTHOR) where a language model reads an ordered list: a Research agent that synthesizes five agent votes into one directional vote. Using the production prompt, 24 synthetic evidence sets in three strata, and 3,840 calls to deepseek-flash at temperature 0, we compare all 120 orderings of each set against 40 repeats of one fixed ordering, so that order effects are measured against the model's own noise. The mean diversity increase under permutation is 0.028 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.042 within the amended two-test family; not significant under the originally registered four-test family). The point estimate is below the pre-registered smallest effect size of interest (0.05), but effects of that size cannot be excluded, and equivalence is not shown; the registered verdict is inconclusive. We find no evidence of a primacy or recency effect (p = 0.49). Intrinsic noise is large where evidence conflicts: under an identical input, the modal direction in the balanced-conflict stratum is returned in only 72% of repeats. Traced through a replica of the production aggregator, no change in the synthesizer's output direction altered any consensus result: by construction of the stimuli and the rule, consensus is unreachable in 15 of the 16 conflict sets whatever the synthesizer outputs, and all 43 observed changes arose from confidence variation in a single near-threshold set. At this boundary the practical risk is nondeterminism rather than order, and how much of it reaches a decision depends on the aggregation rule, the weight it assigns, and where inputs fall relative to its threshold.
why: Pre-registered LLM order sensitivity in live trading system ZVAKTHOR

title: When Stress Tests Miss the Risk: Statistical Scenario Analysis for Financial Portfolios
abstract: Scenario analysis is widely used to stress test financial portfolios, yet conventional approaches often summarize scenario gains using point estimates that overlook dependence between stressed and unstressed risk factors. We develop a machine learning framework for quantifying uncertainty in realized next-day scenario gains through prediction intervals whose widths can be calibrated online. Adaptive conformal scenario analysis (ACSA) calibrates scenario-specific quantile predictions and provides a longrun empirical coverage guarantee over realized scenarios. Our main method, kernel scenario analysis (KSA), estimates scenario-conditional quantiles directly from the specified stress and current market information. KSA can also be combined with ACSA to obtain online-calibrated prediction intervals. In experiments designed to reflect real-world markets, conventional scenario analysis can substantially understate risk, including for portfolios that appear safe under standard stress tests. Our proposed methods achieve better calibration and sharper intervals than empirical-quantile baselines. Overall, the framework moves scenario analysis beyond point estimates by quantifying predictive uncertainty and providing tools for statistically validating scenario gains.
why: Conformal scenario analysis with empirical coverage guarantee for portfolio risk

title: Adaptive State Representation and Critical Explainability Evaluation for A2C-Based Algorithmic Carbon Allowance Trading
abstract: European Union Allowances (EUA), the tradable permits underlying the EU Emissions Trading System, have become a financial asset with regime-dependent price dynamics, motivating algorithmic trading research on this instrument. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) trading agents typically rely on static, uniformly weighted state representations and are often evaluated with limited rigor: no baseline comparison, a single train/test split, single-seed reporting, and claimed interpretability illustrated but not critically tested. We address these gaps with an advantage actor-critic (A2C) agent built around a regime-gated dual-attention (feature and temporal) adaptive state representation, trained under a walk-forward protocol with validation-only model and hyperparameter selection. The agent is evaluated against five classical baselines under identical frictions and test dates, an ablation isolating the adaptive mechanism, a multi-seed robustness study, and a multi-lens explainability analysis. The proposed agent achieves the highest risk-adjusted return and win rate among all evaluated strategies, with a Sharpe ratio of $2.45$. An ablation isolates the adaptive representation as the cause of a further gain in return and risk-adjusted performance, together with a marked reduction in maximum drawdown relative to an otherwise identical non-adaptive agent. A multi-seed evaluation indicates that performance is sensitive to random initialization, highlighting the variability and limited robustness of the results across different runs; this limitation is explicitly acknowledged. A critical explainability evaluation further shows feature and temporal attention to be largely stable across market regimes and actions, rather than sharply regime-adaptive as originally hypothesized.
why: A2C trading with walk-forward validation and ablation, rigorous eval

title: Abstention Is Not Neutral: Ablating the LLM in an LLM Trading Agent
abstract: Abstention by a language-model trading agent is not neutral: the agents do not disagree with the rule that has their inputs, they abstain, and for an agent that holds a position an abstention is a sale avoided. We run a preregistered paper-trading system in which three agents decide daily trades in five ETFs beside the moving-average rule on the same price inputs. In 262 live and 2,173 anonymised historical decisions the agents opposed the rule in 0% and 1.1% of cases, with no detectable gain. A larger model, on 300 points that over-represent days on which the close is within two per cent of a long-term (150-day) moving average, opposed it 1 time and abstained on 80% of those days. A calendar of scheduled macroeconomic events changed 64 decisions, 59 of them into abstentions; this is a change of behaviour, and we find no improvement in quality. Live, the agent ledgers and the rule ledgers hold different positions on about one asset-day in five, and the consensus gate between agents blocked 22 decisions, all of them sales. The abstention depends on one sentence of the prompt: replacing it with an instruction to commit lowers the abstention rate from 55% to 19%, and the released decisions follow the rule. The same input sent twice changes 9% of decisions. We propose a minimal evaluation protocol for agent papers. The results cover two models from one provider and a short live record.
why: Pre-registered LLM agent test; negative result shows no improvement from abstention

title: Residual Learning in Empirical Asset Pricing
abstract: Shallow models are special cases of deep models, and deep models theoretically have the potential to outperform the shallow ones. However, the existing empirical asset pricing literature provides strong benchmarks for shallow models. Residual learning allows neural network models in asset pricing to go deeper by preserving and refining their shallow counterparts. The out-of-sample Sharpe ratio for value-weighted long-short portfolios of deep residual models (2.07) is higher than that for the corresponding shallow ones (1.92) and more than twice that of the deep feedforward models (0.89). We show that model depth is a source of additional economic value in asset pricing. Residual learning can be used to deepen other neural-network-based asset pricing models if they contain intermediate layers. Our design also provides one way to scale asset pricing models, making native "large asset pricing models" more feasible.
why: Out-of-sample Sharpe ratios, residual learning beats baseline

title: From Word Counts to Context: Topic Models for Asset Pricing
abstract: News may reveal systematic risk, but whether its context enhances the construction of systematic risk factors is still unclear. We seek to test whether utilizing a sentence transformer represents an improvement over techniques such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) in the coherence of topic term lists generated from unstructured text data. To test this, the same collection of unstructured text data comprising of 394,661 articles and the same downstream financial portfolio construction pipeline were applied with the text layer differing, including the length of article text each model used and how topic terms were ranked: we benchmark LDA against a frozen sentence transformer with k-means clustering. We find that the sentence transformer branch had higher observed scores both in terms of coherence (measured by NPMI) as well as financial performance (measured by Sharpe), although the available tests do not establish outperformance. Further exploratory specifications such as utilizing spherical clustering and multi-horizon exposures had an observed excess-return Sharpe of 1.03 for the combined model. We believe that there is some promise in applying context-aware techniques on unstructured news text, but stricter tests using only information available at each date and broader datasets may be required to enhance the confidence in the observed performance.
why: Sentence transformers beat LDA on asset pricing Sharpe, real financial test

title: The Mirror of Erised: Misperception of Foreign Economic Policy Uncertainty and Stock Market Volatility
abstract: Does Chinese media misperceive U.S. economic policy conditions? We propose a U.S. economic policy uncertainty index perceived by Chinese media. This index exhibits notable divergence from the U.S. economic policy uncertainty index reported by U.S. media. Article-level evidence from BERTopic attributes this discrepancy primarily to Chinese media misperception of the sources and magnitude of U.S. economic policy uncertainty. Empirical results show that the U.S. EPU perceived by Chinese media exert a significant positive impact on Chinese stock volatility, whereas the U.S. EPU reported by U.S. media does not. This positive effect remains significant after controlling China-specific policy and is more pronounced among large, young, high transparent, non-manufacturing, and low trade dependency firms. Leveraging the large language model (LLM) to extract textual information and capture emotional changes, we identify two underlying mechanisms explaining this effect: concerns among corporate management and investors’ overconfidence in private information valuation induced by Chinese media misperception about the U.S.
why: Chinese media misperception of US EPU predicts stock volatility, NLP signal

title: Governed AI for the total portfolio approach: factor, macro and tail-risk lenses
abstract: The total portfolio approach (TPA) asks asset owners to judge every position by its contribution to total-fund objectives rather than within asset-class silos. That ambition creates an analytical burden that AI systems are increasingly proposed to carry. This letter argues that AI can make TPA operational only if it is embedded in a governed process rather than treated as an autonomous optimizer. We propose a seven-step governed AI process built on executable mandate objects, a firewall and action budgets, and map it onto the TPA decision cycle. We specify three lenses that the process must run on every candidate portfolio: factor exposures, macro-regime scenarios, and holistic tail risk measured by both value-at-risk (VaR) and expected shortfall (ES). A stylized, synthetic illustration shows that candidates scaled to the same 10% volatility differ sharply in factor composition (equity drives 33% to 95% of baseline variance), that a stagflation-type correlation shift raises volatility from 10% to between 11.1% and 11.9% (relative increases of 11.3% to 18.5%), and that ES at 97.5% exceeds VaR at 99% by about 6.6% under fat tails but not under a Gaussian assumption. We close with three testable propositions and a research agenda. The contribution is conceptual; we claim no empirical validation.
why: Portfolio framework with factor/macro/tail-risk lenses; framework not empirical test.

title: Dynamic Graph Neural Networks for Real Time Systemic Risk Surveillance: An Explainable AI Framework for Financial Stability
abstract: Systemic risk in interconnected financial networks remains a critical threat to global economic stability, repeatedly exposing the profound limitations of traditional, static econometric models. Existing risk surveillance approaches largely fail to capture the dynamic, temporal evolution of interbank relationships and critically lack the interpretability required for practical regulatory adoption. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel Dynamic Graph Neural Network (DGNN) framework equipped with temporal attention mechanisms designed explicitly for real-time systemic risk surveillance. This predictive architecture is fundamentally augmented with an integrated Explainable AI (XAI) module that provides node-, edge-, and feature-level transparency, rendering its complex predictions interpretable for macro-prudential oversight. Extensive empirical evaluation on a comprehensive US FDIC Call Report dataset spanning 2010 to 2024, encompassing approximately 8,000 financial institutions, demonstrates the superior efficacy of our approach. Our framework achieves an Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) of 0.847, providing a robust early warning lead time of 3 to 4 quarters ahead of systemic distress events and significantly outperforming state-of-the-art static baselines. By operationalizing transparent, AI-driven macro-prudential oversight, this research significantly advances financial stability and explicitly aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, specifically fostering strong, accountable institutions (SDG 16) and promoting resilient, inclusive economic growth (SDG 8).
why: Systemic risk surveillance framework, solid but regulatory not execution focus.

title: Which Firms Will Become High ESG Performers? Evidence from Machine Learning
abstract: This study employs machine learning models to predict high ESG performers and utilizes explainable AI to identify their underlying characteristics. We construct a panel dataset covering 1,186 publicly listed U.S. firms from 2006 to 2021, integrating 33 variables, including financial indicators, CEO attributes, linguistic features from 10-K reports, stock returns, and ESG incident data. Our findings show that the machine learning models outperform the traditional Logit model in predicting high ESG performers, demonstrating higher predictive accuracy. Key drivers of high ESG performers include firm size, CEO ownership, payout ratio, leverage, and R&D intensity, which are primarily financial and governance-related factors. Notably, firms accurately classified as high ESG performers by the machine learning model tend to share common characteristics such as large firm size, shareholder-friendly capital policies, low leverage, forward-looking narratives, and younger CEOs.
why: ML predicts ESG scores, but unclear financial relevance or outcome

title: Break-Adjusted GARCH Versus Deep Learning: Multi-Horizon Volatility Forecasts for Kenyan Equity, Currency and Global Oil Markets
abstract: This study compares break-adjusted GARCH and deep-learning approaches to forecasting volatility in Brent crude oil spot prices, the USD/KES exchange rate and the NSE 20 Share Index. Daily returns are examined for variance shifts using a heteroskedasticity-robust modified ICSS procedure. Expanding-window, rolling-window and break-adjusted GARCH forecasts are evaluated alongside neural-network forecasts at 1-, 20-, 60-and 120-trading-day horizons using rolling-origin validation and multiple loss measures. Two significant variance breaks are identified for the NSE 20 Share Index and six for USD/KES; none is detected for Brent, despite conspicuous crisis-period volatility. For the equity series, the FIGARCH persistence parameter declines from 0.259 (p = .017) before break adjustment to 0.142 (p = .382) afterwards, indicating that structural change explains part of the apparent long memory. Forecast rankings vary across markets, horizons and loss measures. Break-adjusted GARCH and FIGARCH are competitive at the one-day horizon for equities and USD/KES, respectively, whereas CNN-LSTM performs strongly at longer equity horizons and LSTM leads the reported longer-horizon USD/KES comparisons. Conventional GARCH variants remain competitive for Brent at longer horizons. By evaluating variance breaks, persistence and multi-horizon predictive accuracy within a common framework, the study shows why neither parameter stability nor the general superiority of deep learning should be assumed in forecasting volatility is a frontier-market. Its findings support asset-specific model selection and regular reassessment after volatility shifts.
why: Kenya volatility forecasting; solid methodology but narrow single-country scope

title: Learning under Imbalance, Volatility and Scarcity: A Synthesis of Adversarial, Language-Based and Knowledge-Driven Systems (2026)
abstract: Eight outputs from 2026 share one problem: building dependable decision support when data are imbalanced, volatile, unstructured or tacit. This paper synthesises them in three groups: adversarial learning for predictive maintenance and stock forecasting, languagebased classification of misinformation and wildfire reports, and knowledge-driven frameworks for organisational decision systems. Reported evidence is compared, not rerun. Specialising one generator per failure type raised PR-AUC from 0.835 (cost-sensitive Random Forest) to 0.857 on the AI4I 2020 benchmark, at about 14 hours of compute. A sentiment-conditioned GAN gave the lowest RMSE on three of seven U.S. equities, so its advantage is asset-dependent. In Greek wildfire social sensing, fine-tuned encoders reached F2 = 0.911 against 0.750 for the best large language model tested, and spatiotemporal disambiguation lifted geocoding accuracy from 54.68% to 80.58%. The two knowledge-management papers are conceptual and not yet tested empirically. Across the studies, metrics were matched to the cost of error, leakage was controlled, and no single model won everywhere. Small test partitions, overlapping stock-forecasting papers and dependence on external services limit the conclusions.
why: Synthesis of multiple domains, lacks coherent financial focus

title: PolicyAgent: A Multi-Agent Generative AI Framework for Automated Reasoning Checks and Policy-Constrained Compliance in Financial Services
abstract: Policy-constrained generative AI in financial services sits at the intersection of two regulatory regimes that disagree on almost everything except cost of failure: a model can be plausibly correct and yet violate Know Your Customer (KYC), suitability, fair-lending, or recordkeeping obligations in ways that scale with throughput. Existing safety layers, whether prompt-engineered guardrails or static keyword filters, neither prove compliance nor leave the audit trail an examiner will eventually ask for. We present PolicyAgent, a five-agent generative AI framework that couples retrieval over a structured policy corpus with formal automated reasoning checks and tamper-evident audit. A Policy Ingestion and Indexing Agent (PIIA) compiles institutional policy documents into a typed reasoning graph; a Reasoning Verification Agent (RVA) discharges per-response obligations through an Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) automated-reasoning backend; a Generative Drafting Agent (GDA), built on a 13B Code-Llama variant fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), produces responses constrained by the RVA feasibility envelope; an Audit Trail Orchestrator (ATO) records every action in a SHA-256 chained, append-only log; and a Continuous Policy Evaluation Coordinator (CPEC) runs the FinPolicyBench evaluation harness against the live system. Evaluated on FinPolicyBench, a reproducible benchmark of 47,200 policy-constrained queries spanning seven obligation categories across a 90-day controlled Continuous Integration / Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline, PolicyAgent achieves a policy-compliance F1 of 0.926, a 71.3% reduction in policy violations per 1,000 responses relative to a prompt-guardrail baseline, a mean reasoning-discharge latency of 412 ms, and a Policy Compliance Score Pi = 0.918, with full ablation studies confirming each agent contributes independently. All quantitative results are simulation-derived: the evaluation uses synthetic and public-text inputs in a controlled CI/CD simulation, with no live customer data and no production deployment; live-deployment validation remains the primary open problem.
why: Compliance governance; not trading or portfolio construction

title: Using LLM Chaining for Enhanced Fraud Detection in Credit Card Transactions: A Multi-Stage Approach
abstract: Credit card fraud represents a $28.58 billion annual challenge globally, with traditional detection systems struggling to adapt to evolving fraud patterns while maintaining low false positive rates. This paper introduces a novel four-stage Large Language Model (LLM) chaining framework for credit card fraud detection that sequentially processes transaction preprocessing, behavioral analysis, risk assessment, and decision synthesis. Our approach leverages the reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs through carefully orchestrated prompt engineering and context management techniques. Experimental evaluation on a comprehensive dataset of 2.1 million transactions demonstrates significant performance improvements, achieving 94.7% accuracy with only 2.1% false positive rate compared to traditional methods. The system provides human-interpretable explanations addressing regulatory compliance requirements while demonstrating superior detection of sophisticated fraud patterns including account takeover scenarios and synthetic identity fraud. Our cost-benefit analysis reveals a 1,153% ROI despite higher computational requirements, making it economically viable for large-scale deployment.
why: LLM chaining for fraud detection; domain different from trading.

title: The Evolution of Business Valuation in the AI Era: Integrating Unstructured Alternative Data into Quantitative Models
abstract: Business valuation has traditionally relied on discounted cash flow (DCF), comparable-company analysis, and other frameworks that translate financial information into estimates of future cash flows, risk, and relative value. Artificial intelligence (AI) does not eliminate these underlying valuation principles, but it can alter how valuation inputs are collected, transformed, and forecast. This narrative review examines three closely related developments: the use of unstructured and alternative data, machine-learning methods for valuation and forecasting, and explainable AI (XAI) for model oversight. The literature suggests that alternative data can provide more timely information about firms and markets, while natural language processing (NLP) can convert textual sources such as filings and earnings-call transcripts into measurable signals. Domain-specific language models, including FinBERT, illustrate the potential of financial sentiment analysis, although textual signals remain sensitive to context, measurement choices, and data quality. Evidence from machine-learning research also indicates that nonlinear models can improve relative valuation and peer selection when relationships among fundamentals are complex. At the same time, the literature does not support a blanket conclusion that AI produces superior intrinsic valuations in all settings. Model risk, data leakage, instability, interpretability, governance, and the distinction between prediction and economic valuation remain important limitations. The emerging role of the financial analyst is therefore better understood as one of model stewardship: combining financial theory, data science, validation, and professional judgment. The review concludes with research directions concerning data standards, uncertainty estimation, explainability, and human oversight.
why: Narrative review of valuation—rejected survey format

title: Artificial Intelligence in Investment Portfolio Management: A Comparison Review with Traditional Financial Methods
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping investment portfolio management by enabling nonlinear learning, dynamic allocation and the processing of high-dimensional market information. Yet greater model complexity does not necessarily produce superior investable performance. This study conducts a structured comparative review of traditional portfolio methods and recent AI-based approaches, focusing on return, risk-adjusted performance, transaction costs and turnover, market-regime robustness, explainability and implementation feasibility. The review combines foundational portfolio theory with recent peer-reviewed evidence on machine learning, deep learning, deep reinforcement learning, automated model selection and cost-aware optimization. The synthesis shows that AI can improve representation, forecasting and adaptive allocation, especially in dynamic and high-dimensional settings, but apparent gains can disappear after realistic trading frictions, unstable training or regime shifts. Traditional methods therefore remain important benchmarks and portfolio-control mechanisms. Building on the evidence, the study proposes a six-dimensional evaluation framework and an evidence-derived hybrid architecture in which AI supports signal generation and regime detection while constrained financial optimization governs allocation, risk and implementation. The main contribution is an integrated decision protocol that shifts comparison from isolated predictive or gross-return performance toward investable decision quality. Future research should validate the framework and architecture on common datasets, multiple market regimes and harmonized transaction-cost assumptions, reporting both gross and net-of-cost performance
why: Structured review of AI portfolio methods—rejected survey

title: From Debiasing to Behavioral Reconfiguration: Artificial Intelligence and Retail Investor Decision-Making
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in retail investment decision-making, yet the behavioural consequences of AI-assisted investing remain fragmented across robo-advice, algorithmic advice and emerging generative-AI research. This systematic review synthesises 99 peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2026 using a PRISMA-guided search, structured evidence extraction and thematic synthesis. The evidence does not support a uniform debiasing effect. Instead, AI can attenuate, amplify, reconfigure or leave unchanged behavioural mechanisms depending on system design, investor characteristics and decision context. Six themes emerge: selective debiasing and portfolio discipline; behavioural amplification and reconfiguration; trust, resistance and calibrated reliance; human-AI interaction and social cues; investor heterogeneity and vulnerability; and information processing, delegation and GenAI cognitive partnership. The review identifies trust and reliance as central transmission mechanisms and distinguishes conventional robo-advice from interactive GenAI, where cognitive assistance can coexist with metacognitive risks such as inflated self-assessed ability. An integrative framework links AI/platform and investor/context characteristics to cognitive and affective mechanisms, reliance states, behavioural consequences and investment outcomes. The review contributes a conditional behavioural-finance account of AI-assisted investing and develops a structured agenda for future research on investor welfare, calibrated reliance and human-AI decision-making.
why: Systematic review of AI and investor behavior—rejected survey

title: A Unified Stochastic-Regulatory-Machine Learning Framework for MedTech Equity Valuation
abstract: We develop a unified stochastic–regulatory–machine learning framework for valuing MedTech equities, integrating seven interacting layers: (I) a Heston Bates stochastic-volatility-with-jumps process for the underlying price dynamics; (II) a hidden Markov regime-switching model, filtered via the Wonham equation, to capture discrete transitions across clinical and regulatory phases; (III) a compound real-options lattice for valuing the multi-stage R&D pipeline against FDA stage-gate decisions; (IV) a stochastic Lanchester–McKendrick system modelling competitive market-share attrition between incumbent and disruptor firms; (V) an ICER-linked value-based-pricing constraint that transmits health economic reimbursement signals into the equity drift; (VI) an ARFIMA–LSTM hybrid that decomposes returns into a long-memory linear component and a learned nonlinear residual; and (VII) an Unscented Kalman Filter for online joint state-parameter estimation. We derive the model’s risk-neutral dynamics under a measure change satisfying Novikov’s condition, prove existence and uniqueness of a strong solution to the coupled SDE system via a Yamada Watanabe argument and a global Lyapunov function, and establish that the resulting discounted price process is an equivalent-martingale-measure price consistent with no-arbitrage. We further characterise the market as incomplete, arising from unspanned variance, jump, regime, and competitive risk, and propose a minimum-entropy martingale measure as a canonical pricing rule, together with an entropic robustness adjustment over a Kullback–Leibler ball of alternative measures. Asymptotic consistency of the Unscented Kalman Filter is established under standard filter-stability and observability conditions. The resulting unified pricing functional aggregates the Heston–Bates component, pipeline real-option values, a competitive-position premium, a value-based-pricing penalty, and a machine-learning residual correction into a single closed-form decomposition, offering a tractable yet theoretically grounded approach to MedTech equity valuation under regulatory, competitive, and reimbursement uncertainty.
why: Seven-layer valuation model; theoretical without empirical test evidence.

title: Privacy-Preserving Financial Income Classification Privacy-Preserving Financial Income Classification Using Federated Learning: A Critical Review of Current Approaches, Challenges, and Context-Aware Solutions
abstract: The rapid adoption of machine learning in financial services has created opportunities for automated income classification, credit assessment, customer segmentation, fraud detection, and risk analysis. These applications depend on sensitive financial and socioeconomic information, creating a tension between analytical utility and privacy protection. Centralized machine-learning architectures can concentrate sensitive records in a single environment and increase the consequences of unauthorized access, compromise, or secondary use. Privacy-preserving machine learning has consequently attracted substantial research attention, with federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and context-aware privacy mechanisms offering complementary forms of protection. This critical review examines these approaches in relation to financial income classification and synthesizes the principal strengths, limitations, and unresolved design problems identified in the author's dissertation. Federated learning reduces the need to transfer raw financial records by keeping training data at participating institutions, but it does not by itself guarantee privacy because model updates can support inference, gradient leakage, or poisoning attacks. Differential privacy can reduce disclosure risk by perturbing model updates, but stronger privacy can reduce model utility and increase computational or communication costs. Context-aware privacy introduces an adaptive dimension by allowing protection to respond to data sensitivity, trust, network security, device integrity, and user role. The synthesis indicates that these mechanisms are often treated separately, leaving a gap in integrated, adaptive privacy control for distributed financial income classification. The paper therefore proposes a conceptual hybrid framework that combines federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and a context-aware privacy decision engine. The proposed direction is intended to balance privacy, classification performance , communication efficiency, scalability, and security rather than optimizing any single objective in isolation.
why: Privacy-preserving learning review—rejected survey format

title: An Enterprise Portfolio Probabilistic Decision-Analytic Methodology that Unifies Planning and Operational Execution
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to introduce a fully integrated, risk-informed, probabilistic framework that carries over seamlessly from enterprise portfolio decision making to operational risk and opportunity management. It accomplishes this function by adhering to the following six principles and premises: (1) that quantitative, probabilistic risk analysis and management methods need to be used not only at the level of projects and programs, but also for enterprise portfolio planning and execution; (2) that success at enterprise level requires continuously considering not only the financial, safety, security, and technical gains that emanate from mission accomplishment, but also potential aspirational gains that are not directly quantifiable at the time planning occurs; (3) that the consideration of aspirational gains requires tapping into the insights and tacit knowledge of stakeholders and other affected parties by introducing and applying affective performance measures (e.g., their degrees of enthusiasm or concern); (4) that a key element of the analysis should be the initial derivation of an integrated resource allocation scheme and its subsequent updating to continually optimize the balance between competing objectives; (5) that the first four premises motivate the use of Monte Carlo methods to account for all important sources of uncertainty; and (6) that the overall methodology should be extendable to decision-making arenas that require national and international cooperation such as AI and climate change. The paper presents a formalism that accommodates these and other related principles and premises and demonstrates how the results of the analyses can be effectively communicated to management.
why: Portfolio risk framework paper, limited practitioner application

title: AI as a Business: Like the Airlines, but Much, Much Worse? Capital Intensity, Depreciation, and the Chimera of Capturing the Gains
abstract: Artificial intelligence will become one of the largest and most useful industries in history. That is hard to doubt. What this paper argues is that, unless demand at cost-based prices proves large enough to fill the capacity now being built, many of the firms that build its infrastructure will fail to earn their cost of capital. The right comparison for those firms is then not Microsoft or Google in their prime but the airlines, only much, much worse. On the dimension that matters most, the speed at which capital must be bought again, AI is much worse than an airline. Accelerators have an economic life of four to five years, against decades for an airframe. Under the paper's illustrative asset mix, an installed AI infrastructure stock of about $3.8 trillion, a conservative figure beside current estimates of spending, some 60 percent of it compute and the rest power plant and buildings, needs roughly $600 billion a year merely to replace depreciating capital. Trivial arithmetic then shows that such an enterprise must bring in on the order of $1.1 to $1.3 trillion of revenue a year to clear a cost of capital between 8 and 12 percent, and close to $900 billion merely to replace itself and cover its operating costs at a zero return. The shortfall against the cost of capital survives compute lives as long as eight years. But there are multiple forces pushing prices well below that. Frontier capabilities converge, so suppliers become fungible. Learning routers make model identity irrelevant, competition commoditizes the routers, and portable compilers weaken hardware lock-in. And much industrial demand can wait, so idle compute has to be sold the way an airline sells an empty seat. On sufficiently narrow professional tasks, small models distilled on data the customer owns can approach frontier performance at a small fraction of the cost, so customers can even build their own "planes." The labor savings from automation are real and may run to trillions of dollars a year, but they flow to the buyers of intelligence and, through competition among those buyers, onward to their customers. The builders of the "fleet" face losses on the capital sunk in the buildout. A formal model shows why the survivors should then expect ordinary returns at best. Open weights, which no bankruptcy removes, turn the supply of intelligence below the open frontier into an approximately free-entry business wherever serving is standardized, and a rival paid by a complementary business can rationally run the token business at a loss.
why: AI industry economics and capital intensity; finance analysis not ML.

title: Strategic Bidding of Heterogeneous Generators in Sequential Electricity and Environmental Markets via Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Environmental markets reshape the bidding incentives of generators, but learning strategic offers under incomplete information is challenging when thermal and renewable units have different controllable decisions and must satisfy shared environmental requirements. This paper develops a stylized sequential electricity–environmental market model and a constrained bounded-action multi-agent proximal policy optimization (CB-MAPPO) method for heterogeneous generators. At each simulated hour, a network-constrained electricity market clears segmented offers. Locational marginal prices are recovered by fixing the block-acceptance decisions and re-solving the continuous clearing problem. Tradable green certificates, eligible carbon offsets, and carbon allowances are then settled in sequence without revising the cleared dispatch. The environmental payoff adjusts the reference cost of the following hour’s offer, linking settlement to subsequent bidding. Thermal generators choose a basic price adjustment, an inter-block price increment, and a total offered quantity; renewable generators submit their available output and control only price-related actions. CB-MAPPO uses bounded stochastic policies to generate these unit-specific actions and adaptive penalties to incorporate carbon intensity, renewable utilization, and average electricity price into training. Centralized training and decentralized execution allow each generator to bid using its local observations and public market information. Simulations with ten strategic generators on the IEEE 39-bus system show that full market coupling reduces carbon emissions by 10.0% and increases renewable utilization by 32.9 percentage points relative to the electricity-only configuration. These results demonstrate how environmental feedback and heterogeneous bidding decisions jointly affect market outcomes.
why: Energy market simulation, not financial markets

title: STASH: A Composable AI-Powered Architecture for Personalized Financial Management
abstract: As the digital economy becomes increasingly fragmented, it has become much more challenging for users to keep their financial information in one place and maintain a comprehensive view of their personal finances. The ability for users to have a full view of their wealth has been impacted by cognitive overload. This cognitive overload is compounded by the existing solutions that require manual data entry; have rigid rule-based classifications, which fail on ambiguous merchant names (e.g., "Swiggy Instamart"); and are based on unscalable monolithic architecture. We have developed STASH, which is an ethereal, composable finance platform that helps to addresses all these shortcomings with its decoupled architecture. STASH uses Google Gemini 1.5-Flash to classify transactions at zero-shot; it intelligently automates the data entry from receipt images using the receipt-text feature and natural language processing. STASH has a three-layer security model and event-driven workflows for handling background processes, which means that AI inference is not at the expense of responsiveness to the user. Performance tests on a standard broadband internet connection showed that the average dashboard load latency was 2.22 seconds. This work demonstrates that Composable, AI-Driven Architectures will provide a more maintainable and scalable architecture for production-ready FinTech applications than traditional monolithic architectures.
why: Personal fintech transaction classification, not financial markets

title: AI Financial Literacy and Financial Peace: A Moderated Mediation Analysis of Financial Confidence and Financial Resilience
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping personal financial management by enabling access to intelligent financial advice, automated budgeting, and personalized investment services. Although financial literacy has been studied extensively in traditional and digital contexts, limited empirical evidence explains how AI Financial Literacy (AIFL) contributes to individual Financial Peace (FP) and the psychological mechanisms underlying this relationship. This study examines the direct and indirect effects of AIFL on FP through Financial Confidence (FC), while testing Financial Resilience (FR) as a moderator, using Hayes' PROCESS Model 7. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was employed; a structured five-point Likert questionnaire yielded 344 valid responses from users of AI-enabled financial services. Cronbach's alpha and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) confirmed the reliability and validity of the measurement instrument. The results show that AIFL significantly enhances FC, and FC positively influences FP. However, the direct effect of AIFL on FP was not significant, indicating that FC fully mediates this relationship. FR significantly strengthens the effect of AIFL on FC, and the Index of Moderated Mediation confirms that the indirect effect of AIFL on FP through FC becomes stronger as FR increases. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, the study positions AIFL as a technological extension of financial capability and demonstrates how it is translated into psychological financial outcomes through confidence and resilience. The findings offer actionable guidance to policymakers, financial institutions, and Fin-Tech developers designing AI-based financial education programs aimed at building financial confidence and resilience among consumers.
why: Behavioral psychology survey, off-topic for trading practitioner

title: Beyond Access: The Hidden Financial Inclusion Gap in America — and What the Next Inclusion Architecture must Achieve
abstract: The United States has achieved very high levels of formal banking access, yet account ownership and digital availability do not by themselves establish meaningful financial inclusion. This paper examines the gap between formal access and effective financial participation and develops a multidimensional framework based on Access, Usage, Quality, and Outcomes. Using the June 2023 Current Population Survey Unbanked/Underbanked Supplement, the paper reproduces the conventional U.S. banking gap of 18.4 percent of households and develops an outcome-inclusive Meaningful Financial Inclusion Gap. Under the central specification, approximately 25.0 percent of U.S. households—about 33.5 million households—exhibit a meaningful inclusion deficit. A broader Inclusion Opportunity encompasses approximately 35.5 percent of households, or about 47.5 million households, whose observable circumstances may justify more relevant or timely financial assistance without necessarily classifying them as financially excluded. The paper also identifies a separate youth and future-inclusion dimension and examines financial inclusion among small businesses, nonemployer firms, and gig workers. The analysis further considers digital inclusion, banking deserts, fragmented financial-service distribution, household financial coordination, artificial intelligence, open-data infrastructure, regulatory accountability, and the role of financial capability across the life course. It argues that the next stage of financial inclusion should focus not only on whether financial products are available, but on whether people and businesses can discover, understand, access, use, and benefit from appropriate financial services while retaining transparency, choice, agency, and clear institutional accountability. The paper proposes Hyper-Relevance as a public design principle for more contextually appropriate financial assistance while intentionally excluding any proprietary technical, commercial, or implementation architecture.
why: Banking access policy survey, not market-relevant ML

title: Evidence-Grounded Agentic AI for Sensitive U.S. Accounting Workflows: Autonomy Boundaries, Escalation, and Internal Control
abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence systems are entering accounts payable, reconciliation, journal-entry, and estimate workflows that sit inside internal control over financial reporting. Prior accounting research has examined chatbot performance, auditor reliance on algorithmic advice, robotic process automation (RPA) governance, and, more recently, retrieval-augmented assistants. Comparatively limited evidence exists on a different question: when a software agent may complete a U.S. accounting action, when it must obtain human review, when the conclusion is reserved for professional judgment, and when the agent must stop. This paper develops an evidence-grounded multiagent architecture (EGAA) and an Accounting Agent Autonomy Framework (A3F) that map transaction risk, materiality, evidence quality, control constraints, and judgment intensity onto four exclusive actions-AUTO, REVIEW, JUDGMENT, and STOPusing authoritative U.S. sources (FASB/U.S. GAAP, SEC, PCAOB, COSO, NIST, GAO, and AICPA). We release a balanced 96case decision-boundary benchmark spanning four workflows and compare four reproducible configurations. A generic ungrounded agent attains 27.1% decision accuracy, cites fabricated standards in every case, and autonomously acts on 44.8% of judgment or stop items. Retrieval without an autonomy gate does not repair those errors. EGAA raises decision accuracy to 78.1%, eliminates fabricated citations in this harness, and reduces inappropriate autonomy to 2.1%. A conservative human-review overlay further lowers inappropriate autonomy, at the cost of fewer straightthrough AUTO decisions. The results support treating accounting agents as control-sensitive systems whose principal design problem is the decision boundary, not fluency.
why: Accounting automation; not financial markets

title: From Platforms to Decision Architectures: How Agentic AI shapes Digital Market Competition
abstract: Agentic AI is shifting digital competition from matching supply and demand to structuring user decisions. This article identifies three emerging archetypes of agentic competition, integrated, orchestrated, and user-proximate decisioning, building on the strategic trajectories of Amazon, Google, and OpenAI. Based on this typology, we derive implications for research and practice.
why: Market competition framing; position paper, no evidence

title: Accountability Follows Risk: A Policy Design Principle for Governing Agentic AI in Financial Services
abstract: In April 2026, US regulators excluded Agentic AI from model risk guidance while retreating from the prescriptive organisational architecture that made prior guidance effective. This leaves a structural governance gap for autonomous systems that operate across functional boundaries. This paper develops accountability-follows-risk as a policy design principle that addresses this gap. Extending agency theory to multi-layered principal-agent chains involving machine agents, the paper establishes that classical accountability mechanisms become structurally insufficient when delegation chains are multi-layered and information asymmetry is interpretive rather than observational. Through institutional theory, it demonstrates that voluntary structural adaptation is blocked by the same isomorphic pressures that only regulatory action can redirect. The paper operationalises the principle through five structural requirements and demonstrates through regulatory precedent that prescriptive structural governance, delivered through supervisory guidance, produces durable institutional change in financial services.
why: Accountability theory; no empirical content

title: Global Data Center Park -Atacama Desert, Antofagasta Region, Chile: Business, Financing and Regulatory Case -a dry-cooled gigawatt-scale AI compute park, built one gigawatt at a time
abstract: This paper sets out the business, financing and regulatory case for the Global Data Center Park, a proposed AI compute park in the María Elena / Sierra Gorda belt of Chile's Antofagasta Region. The park is built in identical 1 GW increments, each with 4.41 GW of photovoltaic generation, 16.5 GWh of sodium-ion storage and heat rejected to dry desert air through air-cooled condensers. It uses about 106 cubic meters of water a day, against about 31,500 for evaporative cooling. All-in capital cost, including servers, is $50.43bn per increment, $2.24bn below a like-for-like islanded, dry-cooled campus in Texas; Chile's exemption of machinery from property tax widens the gap. The site can hold about 107 increments, but land tenure rather than cost is the binding constraint: one increment needs 1.85 times the land Chile has ever tendered for renewables in one transaction, which is why the park must be built one gigawatt at a time. A single staged environmental approval covering five gigawatt tranches lets tenants take pre-approved capacity and saves them 2.5–3.5 years to first operation. At about 117–118 ms round trip to Los Angeles and New York on existing and planned cable, the park suits training, batch, agentic and reasoning workloads and typed chat. It also covers labor, ports, export licensing and open risks. AI disclosure: The author used an AI assistant (Perplexity Computer) for literature search, drafting, calculation checks and formatting. The author directed the research, reviewed every source and figure, and is responsible for the content.
why: Data center infrastructure case; not financial markets

title: Auditing The Machine: Professional Skepticism As The Template For Value-Added Assessment In Accounting Education Working Paper -September 2026 -Comments Welcome
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now draft audit memos, propose adjusting entries, and answer accounting examination questions at a level approaching-and on some tasks exceedingthat of students. Accounting education has responded largely by policing production: proctoring, detection, and honor codes aimed at keeping the machine out of the assessment. This paper argues the profession should respond instead from its own intellectual tradition. Auditing has institutionalized, for over a century, the precise capability that AI-rich assessment requires: a documented, defensible discipline of not believing output-professional skepticism. Building on two propositions-that the professor's role shifts from transmitting knowledge to developing students' capacity to formulate problems, architect and orchestrate intelligent work, control the epistemic quality of outputs, and remain accountable for consequential judgments, and that assessment should measure the value a student adds above a standardized AI baseline-we re-specify a six-capability pipeline for accounting education and demonstrate a worked implementation in a senior auditing course: baselinereferenced assignments in inherent risk assessment, control reliance, and bundled revenue recognition, a seeded-error workpaper dossier, an orchestration log modeled on working-paper discipline, and a viva structured as a mock regulatory inspection. Implications are drawn for the CPA Evolution curriculum, assurance-of-learning practice, and the preparation of entry-level professionals whose first jobs no longer teach judgment the old way.
why: Accounting pedagogy with AI, not financial ML building

title: ESG Integration and Corporate Financial Resilience in Emerging Markets: The Role of Institutional Quality, Green Innovation, and Financial Constraints
abstract: The Chinese banking sector, comprising more than 4,600 institutions with combined assets exceeding ¥420 trillion as of 2024, confronts escalating pressures from rising non-performing loan (NPL) ratios, intensified regulatory scrutiny under the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission (CBIRC), and the imperative to align with Basel III capital adequacy standards. This study investigates the adoption and impact of big data analytics (BDA) on audit quality and operational efficiency within Chinese commercial banks, drawing upon primary survey data from 413 audit professionals representing 86 banking institutions across 24 provinces and supplementary case studies from six banks spanning state-owned, joint-stock, city commercial, and rural commercial segments. The empirical findings reveal that banks deploying advanced analytics—including gradient-boosted machine learning classifiers, transformer-based natural language processing models, and real-time continuous auditing platforms—achieve a 37.2% improvement in NPL misclassification detection, a 31.6% reduction in total audit engagement hours, and a 43.8% decrease in credit-related financial restatements relative to institutions relying on conventional audit methodologies. Structural equation modeling (SEM) analysis establishes statistically significant relationships between BDA adoption intensity and the composite Audit Quality Index (β = 0.436, p
why: Banking audit operations; not trading or markets

title: LLM-Driven Reward Evolution for Integrated Energy System Scheduling under Ladder-Type Carbon Trading
abstract: Integrated energy system (IES) scheduling under ladder-type carbon trading involves horizon-level carbon settlement, which complicates the design of effective stepwise rewards for reinforcement learning. This paper proposes large language model (LLM)-driven Adaptive Reward Evolution (LLM-ADRE), a training framework for iteratively adapting reward–policy candidates from engineering operating outcomes. A posterior engineering evaluator measures operating cost, accounted emissions, thermal-service deviations, and terminal state-of-charge (SOC) deviation over complete scheduling episodes, providing a common basis for candidate comparison independent of reward-specific returns. Reward relabeling, quality-based rollout allocation, and conditional parameter transfer reuse collected transitions and learned policy information after reward revisions. Across three seeds on a 28-day held-out test set, LLM-ADRE improves mean episode quality by 5.6% over Manual-Reward under the same environment-interaction budget. It also reduces mean accounted emissions and combined thermal-service deviation by 2.14% and 37.96%, respectively, with similar operating cost and terminal SOC deviation. It achieves comparable observed scheduling quality to Eureka while using one-third of Eureka’s nominal environment-interaction budget.
why: Energy system scheduling, off-topic

title: Supply Chain Finance Strategies, Artificial Intelligence Adoption, and Sustainable Performance: The Mediating Role of Supply Chain Resilience in Ghanaian Manufacturing
abstract: Purpose – This study examines how supply chain finance (SCF) strategies and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption influence supply chain resilience and, ultimately, the sustainable performance of manufacturing firms in Ghana. It addresses a critical gap: while SCF and AI are increasingly deployed in emerging economies, the mechanism through which they translate into sustainable outcomes particularly the mediating role of resilience remains underexplored.,Design/methodology/approach – Grounded in the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), the study employs a quantitative, explanatory design. Data were collected from 436 senior supply chain decision-makers across five Ghanaian industrial hubs via structured questionnaires. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) tested direct and mediated relationships, complemented by Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA) to identify critical enablers.,Findings – SCF strategies (account financing, trade credit and buyer-direct financing) significantly enhance sustainable performance. Invoice discounting, however, does not exert a direct effect on sustainable performance. Among AI adoption factors, only performance expectancy exerts a direct effect; effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions operate exclusively through resilience. Supply chain resilience is a powerful mediator, channelling the effects of both SCF and AI adoption towards sustainability. NCA identifies trade credit, account financing, and facilitating conditions as necessary not merely sufficient conditions for high sustainable performance. Notably, redundancy is not a significant resilience dimension in this resource-constrained context.,Originality/value – The study provides one of the first empirical integrations of SCF, AI adoption, and resilience within a developing-economy manufacturing context. It introduces necessity logic to SCF research, demonstrating that certain financial resources are non-negotiable prerequisites. It also challenges the universality of redundancy as a resilience strategy, showing that firms in resource-constrained environments build resilience through agility, flexibility, and collaboration.
why: Survey on supply chain finance adoption effects; SEM design off-topic.

title: Beyond Green Location: Green Relocation as a Transition Pathway for Existing Industrial Assets
abstract: Most research on the renewables pull asks where future green production should be located. This paper asks a different question: when an existing industrial asset reaches a major transition decision, should it be maintained, retrofitted, rebuilt in place, relocated wholly or in part, transitioned in phases, or exited? The paper reframes green relocation as one transition pathway for existing industrial assets rather than as a binary location decision. It distinguishes five domestic transition pathways— Maintain, Retrofit, Rebuild in Place, Relocate and Phased Relocation—and treats Domestic Exit as an outside option. These pathways are described along four underlying dimensions: location, depth of change, scope and timing. Their relative attractiveness is organized by four mechanisms: Pull from alternative locations; Anchor from the accumulated advantages of the incumbent site; Release from automation and physical AI, which can relax location constraints at both origin and destination; and Window from asset-renewal events that make inherited locations contestable. The paper separates firm-level value, national social net benefit and regional distribution, and derives seven testable hypotheses. Its central empirical prediction is a Pull × Window interaction: a given alternative-location advantage should have a stronger effect on relocation as an incumbent asset approaches major renewal. Green relocation is therefore treated not as a policy objective or default outcome, but as one possible pathway within a broader industrial transition choice.
why: Green industrial asset transitions, not financial markets

title: AI and Scholarship in Financial Economics
abstract: I detail the 45-minute process of drafting a submission to the UCLA's Human x AI Finance conference that was held in April 2026. There was no human involved in evaluating the papers. My paper was one of four papers selected from 159 submissions. I focus on the implications for our profession including changes that journals need to make and how we evaluate Ph.D. students as well as the new challenges in faculty promotion cases. I also make recommendations with respect to institutional research integrity rules.
why: Meta-commentary on publishing; not research

title: Machine Labor and Democratic Capital Claims: A Political Economy of Advanced AI
abstract: This paper studies the political economy of a machine-labor economy. Advanced artificial intelligence matters not only because it may raise productivity, but because it can make laborlike services reproducible as capital. Digital AI performs cognitive tasks, physical AI performs embodied tasks, and together they create machine labor embodied in autonomous capital. I develop a model in which citizens supply human labor and hold heterogeneous ownership claims on autonomous capital. A rise in machine-labor task reach lowers the labor share and raises the autonomous-capital share. Under laissez-faire, the median citizen's share of output falls whenever the median citizen is more exposed to labor income than to autonomous-capital ownership. Thus, AI progress can raise the importance of autonomous capital while weakening the median citizen's relative claim on output. Democratic institutional choice then shifts toward claims on autonomous capital. When the median citizen owns less autonomous capital than average, citizen capital claims and AI-rent taxation raise the median citizen's income, and a threshold result shows when a positive citizen claim becomes optimal. If autonomous capital also creates control power over production, information, infrastructure, and access, rising machinelabor task reach increases the median citizen's preferred governance intensity when it raises the marginal benefit of reducing control power. Under joint inward-pointing boundary conditions, the paper identifies an interior institutional region in which private innovation, citizen claims, AI-rent taxation, public AI infrastructure, and democratic governance coexist. The contribution 2 is to show that labor-substituting AI changes not only productivity and factor shares, but the institutional basis of democratic claims on output.
why: Political economy theory, pure theory no data path

title: From ratio calculation to accountable judgment: An OBE-aligned financial statement analysis course with auditable AI use and embedded ethics
abstract: Financial statement analysis projects have long used real companies, peer comparison, staged feedback, and integrated reports to move students beyond ratio calculation. Recent accounting education research has also examined digital tools, generative artificial intelligence (AI), and professional ethics. These strands provide useful resources, but they do not by themselves specify how an instructor can make AI-assisted judgment inspectable while assessing ethical responsibility throughout an authentic analysis. This teaching note describes an outcome-based redesign of an undergraduate course at an application-oriented university in western China. Guided by constructive alignment and cognitive apprenticeship, the design connects five course outcomes to a six-stage listed-company project, staged artifacts, feedback and revision. Students who use AI follow a purpose-record-verify-decide protocol; all students evaluate evidence quality, uncertainty, and stakeholder consequences as part of the financial analysis. The course was delivered in three successive cycles, which supports an account of implementation rather than a claim of learning effectiveness. The contribution is a traceable course architecture, an AI-verification record, a performance rubric, and an adaptation matrix that separates portable design principles from local choices such as reporting standards, case companies, technology access, and external competitions.
why: Accounting education; off-topic

title: Gatekeepers Without Gates? Cloud Computing and the Limits of Qualitative Designation Under the Digital Markets Act
abstract: On June 25, 2026, the European Commission reached the preliminary view that Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure should be designated as gatekeepers under the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Because cloud computing satisfies neither user-number threshold, these would be the first designations based entirely on the DMA’s qualitative criteria. This article argues that the Commission’s position appears to conflate gatekeeping with size. Although cloud services are eligible for designation, Article 3(8) requires each condition to be established independently. Evidence of scale, investment, and economic importance may show that AWS and Azure are “important,” but does not establish that they intermediate between business users and end users as “gateways.” Nor is there clear evidence of entrenchment. Quality-adjusted prices have fallen, market shares have shifted, multihoming is widespread, switching costs have declined, and artificial intelligence has encouraged entry. Predictions that AI, data gravity, or sovereign-cloud requirements will entrench AWS and Azure must satisfy the General Court’s demand in Meta Platforms for specific, contemporaneous reasoning. Proportionality presents a further obstacle. The UK examined the same firms and chose voluntary commitments rather than ex ante regulation, while the EU Data Act provides a switching regime that may constitute a less restrictive alternative. The Commission is still examining whether the DMA’s obligations fit cloud services. The proposed designations will therefore test whether “gatekeeper” remains a distinct legal category for firms controlling competitive bottlenecks, or has become a synonym for “big” or “important.” We argue that the latter interpretation would conflict with the DMA’s goals.
why: Regulatory law analysis; off-topic

title: Accounting for Large Language Masses: A time capsule
abstract: We present the time capsule of an e-mail conversation between the editors and coeditors of this journal that we have painstakingly reconstructed from the data-dust bowl of the late 2020s. Contributions to this conversation illustrate the struggles among journal editors who were dealing with the high number of journal submissions accompanying the arrival of generative AI around that time. They also highlight some of the human eccentricities in figuring out editorial and occupational strategies in a battle for intellectual hegemony which people of that time will have thought they were losing. Whilst some of their despair is shrouded by the articulation of archaic concerns with efficiency or critical scholarship, the undeniable lostness of the human position we now experience will be particularly obvious to the reader in the more confident sounding contributions to this historic debate.
why: Meta-commentary on journal editing; not research

title: The Hound: A Modular and Resilient Framework for Automated Multi-Market Data Extraction in Darknet Environments
abstract: The anonymity and volatility of Darknet Markets (DNMs) present significantbarriers for criminological research and cyber-intelligence. Manual datacollection is often unfeasible due to the short lifespan of onion servicesand sophisticated anti-scraping measures. This paper introducesThe Hound, a robust, automated framework designed for thesystematic extraction and processing of data from multiple Darknet Markets.Built on a modular architecture using Selenium and Tor, the systemsuccessfully navigates authentication challenges and complex web structuresto retrieve structured information on illicit products and vendor activities.We validate our approach through an empirical study involving majormarkets such as AlphaBay, Torzon, Awazon, and Dark Matter, demonstrating theframework's capability to provide reproducible data for long-term patternanalysis. Our results provide insights into market dynamics and offer ascalable foundation for future integration with Natural Language Processing(NLP) for enhanced threat intelligence. The Hound has beenregistered as intellectual property (No.~M-010122/2025, RegistroTerritorial de la Propiedad Intelectual de la Comunidad de Madrid,Universidad Politécnica de Madrid).
why: Darknet market criminology; completely off-topic
